stemMd: Gian Lorenzo Bernini designed the curving colonnade that encloses St Peter's Square in Rome. In which century was it built?
explanationMd:
**What to notice first.** Two things are being tested: which period Bernini belongs to, and how centuries are numbered.

**The fact that settles it.** Bernini (1598-1680) was the leading sculptor and architect of the Roman Baroque. His colonnade for St Peter's Square was built between 1656 and 1667, under Pope Alexander VII.

**The counting step.** The years 1601 to 1700 make up the seventeenth century - in Italian the *Seicento*, 'the six hundreds'. A century's number is one more than the hundreds in its years: for 1656 the hundreds are 16, so the century is the seventeenth.

**How to check it.** Bernini's whole working life falls within the 1600s: he was born in 1598 and died in 1680. Whatever the exact date of the colonnade, it must be a seventeenth-century work.

distractorRationale.d: The fifteenth century is the early Renaissance - the century of Brunelleschi's dome in Florence, completed in 1436. Bernini was not born until 1598.
distractorRationale.a: This is the classic counting slip: reading the first two digits of 1656 as the century number. The sixteenth century covers the years 1501-1600. It is also the century in which Michelangelo designed the dome of St Peter's, which can pull the square back with the basilica, but Bernini's colonnade came decades later.
distractorRationale.c: The eighteenth century is the age of the late Baroque and of works such as the Trevi Fountain (1732-1762). Bernini had died in 1680, so none of his work belongs to it.
distractorRationale.b: The nineteenth century, the age of Neoclassicism and historicist revivals, is almost two centuries after Bernini's death in 1680.

accessibilityText: Question: Gian Lorenzo Bernini designed the curving colonnade that encloses Saint Peter's Square in Rome; in which century was it built? The choices are the sixteenth, nineteenth, eighteenth, fifteenth and seventeenth centuries.

provenance.notes: Original item written for this bank for the TIL-A History and general knowledge section. It combines placing an artist in his period with the century-numbering convention; the sixteenth-century distractor is the off-by-one slip of reading 1656 as the sixteenth century.
